awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Artificial Intelligence Powered Matchmaking and Resource Discovery for University-Driven Innovations
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on an online platform that uses advanced large language model reasoning and natural language processing to match university discoveries with investors, industry partners, and community organizations. The platform collects and studies the full national patent record, open access research papers, and verified inventories of laboratory equipment and other institutional resources. By revealing connections that are currently hidden in separate data silos, the technology addresses the costly delays that slow the transition of research results into new products and services. Across the country thousands of promising inventions remain idle each year because inventors and potential sponsors cannot find one another quickly. Accelerating these matches strengthens the scientific enterprise, supports economic growth, and broadens access to knowledge. Faster adoption of breakthrough health treatments, clean energy devices, and advanced manufacturing methods improves public welfare, creates jobs, and enhances national competitiveness in emerging technology sectors.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a recommendation engine that combines artificial intelligence reasoning with continuously updated knowledge graphs generated from patent filings, scholarly literature, and institutional asset records. The technology is based on interviews with technology transfer professionals, investors, corporate researchers, and community leaders. Insights gained from these engagements guide iterative refinements to algorithms, data pipelines, and user experiences, ensuring that the platform remains accurate, transparent, and straightforward to adopt. Metrics such as search accuracy, match quality, and time to first contact inform technical milestones, while market feedback informs business viability.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Turning a university discovery into a product depends on connecting it with the right partners: companies to develop it, investors to fund it, and experts and facilities to help it mature. Much of this matchmaking still relies on personal networks, conferences, and manual searches of scattered patents, research papers, and clinical trial records, so promising inventions can sit idle because potential partners never find one another.

This NSF I-Corps Teams project explored the commercial potential of DiscoveryHub, an artificial intelligence (AI) platform the team is developing to close this gap. DiscoveryHub is designed to search patents, scientific publications, clinical trials, and other public records, suggest likely partners, and show the evidence behind each suggestion.

What we did

The team included Principal Investigator and Technical Lead Dr. Alex Rudniy, Associate Professor of Computer Science at Drew University; Entrepreneurial Lead Mehek Agrawal, a recent Drew University graduate and early-career data scientist; and Industry Mentor Dr. Charles Lunn, a retired industrial scientist and Fellow of Drew's Research Institute for Scientists Emeriti. Building on an earlier regional I-Corps program at NJIT, the team completed the national I-Corps Teams program in fall 2025. Testing its business assumptions directly with potential customers, the team conducted 115 interviews and attended about 10 industry conferences, trade shows, and partnering events. Interviewees included 36 university technology transfer professionals, 42 business development and research leaders at small, mid-sized, and large life science companies, 10 investors, and 27 consultants and other service providers.

What we learned

We began the program expecting university technology transfer offices to be our first customers. The interviews changed that view: technology transfer staff confirmed the need, but many offices, like many early-stage startups, face tight or shrinking budgets and could not pay for a new tool. Small life science companies had little business development budget beyond conferences, while large companies adopt new tools slowly because decisions pass through many layers of approval. Investors were cautious about very early-stage university technologies, and their expectations often differed from those of academic inventors.

The strongest combination of need and ability to pay came from business development and innovation-scouting teams at mid-sized life science companies. These teams must find and evaluate outside technologies quickly, and they judged a tool mainly by whether it would help existing staff work faster without new hires. Across all groups, protecting confidential information when using AI was a top priority. Interviewees also wanted recommendations that show the evidence behind them, and consistent criteria for comparing opportunities so that serious partners stand out from dead ends.

Intellectual merit

The project turned a broad technical idea into focused research questions grounded in real user needs. Industry scouts describe what they want in clinical and business language, while university patents often describe the same invention in legal or older scientific terms. For example, the cancer immunotherapy target now called PD-L1 appears in a 2004 patent under an earlier name, B7-H1. Early tests of the team's research prototype in summer 2026 showed that bridging these vocabularies is much harder than simple tests suggest, and that fair evaluation requires realistic test questions written the way scouts actually search.

Broader impacts

Faster, better-informed matchmaking can help publicly funded research reach patients and markets sooner, supporting new therapies, jobs, and economic growth. Because DiscoveryHub is designed to draw on public records rather than personal connections, it could also help inventions from institutions and regions outside major innovation hubs reach potential partners. The project gave the Entrepreneurial Lead intensive training in customer discovery and business model design, guided by an experienced industry scientist. It also created research opportunities at Drew University: in summer 2026, students in the Drew Summer Science Institute developed and tested AI search methods for patent and clinical trial data and presented their work at Bergen Community College's STEM C² Research and Career Conference in August. The platform also serves as a reference project in a computer science course.

Outcomes and next steps

The team concluded the program with a decision to move forward: launch a startup that uses grant funding to build and pilot a minimum viable product before seeking private investment, with life science business development teams as the first market. The team then met with potential partners and investors at the 2026 BIO International Convention and in follow-up meetings, and it submitted a Project Pitch to NSF's Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, which it is refocusing on the research questions above for resubmission. Two university technology transfer offices have provided letters of support stating that they will pilot the system once it is funded, and an NSF ACCESS supercomputing allocation supports the team's model development. As the team's lessons-learned video put it, more customers is not better; the right customers are better.
